Attention State Exploration Log

A parallel track to the legacy attention-state pipeline, testing new ways of identifying internal and external attention states from eye movements during movie watching. Each entry is dated and builds on the last.

All figures below show the recomputed features of the fifth entry (vergence from measured samples only, gaze-validity mask) and the robust PCA at lambda 0.05 adopted in the seventh entry. Earlier numbers are kept in those entries for comparison.

guide

The logic, spelled out

The entries below were written as the work happened and use some shorthand. This section defines each piece in order, with the actual numbers, so that the conclusions can be checked step by step.

1. The unit of analysis is a window

Each recording is one person watching one film. It is cut into 236 windows of 10 seconds, stepped every 2.5 seconds, so neighbouring windows overlap by 7.5 seconds. For each window we have eight numbers describing the eyes (saccade rate, saccade dispersion, vergence, vergence variability, blink rate, blink duration, pupil size, pupil variability) and a ninth, ISC, describing how closely that person's gaze followed the group's gaze during the window. Everything in the log is a statement about windows, summarised first within a person and then across people.

2. Standardising within a person

Before anything else, each of the eight eye features is rescaled within each recording: subtract that recording's median, divide by its typical spread. After this a value of +1 means "one typical step above this person's own usual level". A person who always blinks a lot and a person who rarely blinks both end up centred at zero. This is deliberate: the labels are meant to say "unusual for this person", not "unusual compared with other people".

3. How the two clusters were identified

Take all 11,564 windows from all 49 recordings, each described by its eight standardised features, and compute the correlation between every pair of features. That gives 28 correlations. Only three of them are above 0.2 in absolute value:

  • saccade rate and blink rate: r = -0.39 (a window with more saccades tends to have fewer blinks)
  • vergence and vergence variability: r = +0.38
  • vergence and pupil size: r = +0.30

Every other pair sits between -0.1 and +0.2, including every pair that crosses between these two groups: saccade rate with vergence is -0.07, blink rate with pupil is +0.06, and so on. So the features fall into two groups that co-vary inside themselves and not with each other. That is what "two clusters" means. Nothing was fitted to find them; they are visible in the correlation table in the sixth entry.

4. How we know the clusters are distinct

Three checks, all in the sixth entry. First, the cross-cluster correlations listed above are near zero, so movement in one group tells you almost nothing about movement in the other. Second, if you build one score per cluster (blink rate minus saccade rate for the first; vergence plus vergence variability plus pupil for the second) and correlate the two scores within each person across their 236 windows, the average correlation is 0.08. Third, an ordinary principal component analysis, which looks for the direction of largest shared variation, returns the two clusters as its first two components with nearly the same amount of variance, 20 percent and 17 percent, and which one comes first flips between films. If the two groups were one process, PCA would return one strong component and the second would be much smaller. Instead it returns two of similar size, and the "first" one is whichever happened to be slightly larger in that sample.

5. What PC1 is, given that

A principal component is a weighted sum of the eight features. PC1 is the weighted sum that varies most across windows. With two independent clusters of similar size, the weights PC1 lands on are partly arbitrary, and the version the track now uses (robust PCA with the sparse-term weight at 0.05) puts roughly equal weight on both clusters: saccade rate -0.50, blink rate +0.46, vergence +0.43, pupil +0.47. A high PC1 score therefore means "fewer saccades, more blinks, more vergence, larger pupil than usual for this person", with each of those able to contribute. A window can score high because of the saccade-blink pair, because of the vergence-pupil group, or both. The log flags this as a reason to consider labelling on the two clusters separately.

6. What the group deviation is

For each window, take the person's nine features (eight eye features plus ISC) and subtract the average of the other viewers at the same window of the same film. That leaves nine differences: how far this person is from the group on each feature at that moment. The Mahalanobis distance combines the nine into one number, after rescaling them so that a feature that is naturally noisy does not dominate and so that the two clusters count equally. A large distance means the person's combination of eye behaviour is unusual relative to everyone else watching the same scene. This distance is then z-scored within the person, so that "deviation z = +1" means "one typical step further from the group than this person usually is".

7. What "gating PC1 by deviation" means

"Gate" is not a technical term; it is shorthand used throughout this log for the second condition in an "and" rule. The legacy label rule has two conditions. A window is labelled internal only if its PC1 z is above a threshold and its deviation z is above the same threshold. It is labelled external only if PC1 z is below minus the threshold and deviation z is below minus the threshold. The threshold in use is 0.6. Think of it as two steps: PC1 proposes candidate windows, then the deviation condition acts on those candidates and lets some through. That second step is the gate, and the label is what comes out of it. "Gating PC1 by deviation" therefore means: start from the windows PC1 selects, keep only those that also satisfy the deviation condition. The question the log keeps asking is whether that second step changes which windows are kept, or only how many.

Whether a gate is doing anything can be measured. Take the windows PC1 proposes for internal, those with PC1 z above 0.6, which is about 25 percent of all windows. Ask what fraction of them also have deviation z above 0.6. If the two measures were unrelated, that fraction would equal the fraction of all windows with deviation above 0.6, which is about 20 percent. The observed fraction is 41 to 46 percent. So the gate keeps a subset that is twice as likely to be far from the group as a random subset would be: it is selecting on something. Now do the same on the external side. PC1 z below -0.6 is about 29 percent of windows; the fraction of those with deviation below -0.6 is 31 to 35 percent; the fraction of all windows with deviation below -0.6 is 26 to 30 percent. The gate keeps barely more than a random subset would. It discards two thirds of the candidates while changing almost nothing about what they are. That is what "the external gate is uninformative" means.

8. Why the two sides differ

The eighth and ninth entries show the reason directly by cutting PC1 into bins and asking, in each bin, how far from the group the windows are on average. Through the middle of the axis and across the whole external side, windows sit about 0.3 typical steps closer to the group than the person's average. Between PC1 z 0.4 and 0.8 they sit at the person's average. Above 0.8 they move away, reaching one full step beyond average above 1.2. So "high on PC1" and "far from the group" go together only at the internal end. At the external end, windows are not far from the group; they are ordinary. Asking them to be close to the group as well asks for something they already are.

9. Within viewer versus within timepoint

Every z-score above is "within viewer": compared with the same person's other windows. The alternative is "within timepoint": compare the person's value at window 57 with the other viewers' values at window 57, so the question becomes "is this person unusual for this scene" rather than "for themselves". The eighth entry runs the deviation-by-bin analysis both ways and the curves are the same shape. The conclusion about the gate does not depend on which comparison is used.

10. What the region analysis adds

The ninth entry replaces bins with six named regions and tests each claim. Every number is first averaged within a person, so each person contributes one value, and then tested across the 14 to 18 people in a film. "p below 0.001" there means that across people, the mean is reliably different from zero, not that windows were treated as independent. The feature-profile table shows what a window in each region actually looks like in the eight features, and the rule table shows, for six candidate label rules, what the selected windows look like on ISC and on scene-relative deviation. The one row to read with care is the external rule that gates on ISC: its ISC column is high because that is what it selected on, so only its deviation column is evidence.

The short version. Two groups of eye features move independently of each other. PC1 mixes them. Windows high on PC1 are also far from the group, increasingly so above PC1 z 0.8, so requiring both PC1 and deviation for an internal label selects windows that are genuinely unusual. Windows low on PC1 are close to the group already, so requiring low deviation for an external label selects nothing extra and throws away two thirds of the candidates. A small tail of extreme low-PC1 windows, mostly bursts of saccades, is unusual in its own way and should be looked at separately.

2026-09-14

1. Eye-movement features and the gaze PCA without ISC

How the eye-movement features were generated

Binocular gaze was recorded during three movies: Despicable Me in English (17 recordings), the same film dubbed in Hungarian (14), and Inscapes (18). Left and right eye positions were combined, invalid samples were interpolated across short gaps, and saccades and fixations were detected with the REMoDNaV velocity-based classifier. Blinks were taken from the validity signal, keeping events between 90 and 500 ms. Vergence was computed from the horizontal disparity of the two eyes using the screen geometry. Pupil diameter came from the tracker and was rescaled within each individual upstream. Gaze inter-subject correlation (ISC) is the correlation of a viewer's gaze-position trajectory with the rest of the group over the same window.

Every measure was then summarised in 10 s windows stepped every 2.5 s, giving 236 windows per recording aligned to the neural windows.

Saccade_Rate
saccade onsets in the window
Saccade_Dispersion
mean distance from each saccade's onset to the position of the following fixation
Vergence
mean binocular disparity, with Vergence_Std its within-window variability
Blink_Rate
blinks in the window, with Blink_Duration their mean length
Pupil_Avg
mean pupil diameter, with Pupil_Std its within-window variability
ISC
gaze synchrony with the group, carried alongside but not entered into the PCA

Vergence and its variability are computed from measured samples only: where one or both eyes were not tracked the vergence file carries a linear interpolation, and those samples are excluded. A window with fewer than 30% of its samples measured gets no vergence value, and a recording in which vergence is measurable in fewer than half of its windows contributes no vergence at all (five recordings). Windows in which fewer than half the gaze samples were tracked have all eight gaze features set to missing. Before the PCA each of the eight gaze features was standardised within its recording as the deviation from the recording median divided by 1.4826 times the median absolute deviation, so that a few artefactual windows cannot set a recording's scale. Missing values were placed at the recording median. Pupil was left on its upstream per-individual scale, and all ten non-ISC features were then z-scored once across each movie so pupil sits on a comparable scale. Robust PCA separated a sparse outlier component from the feature matrix, and ordinary PCA of the remaining low-rank part gave the components. PC1 was oriented so that high values go with low ISC, keeping the legacy convention that high PC1 indicates internally directed attention.

ISC was excluded from the PCA on purpose. Roughly 55% of its within-recording variance is shared by all viewers at the same moment of the film, so it behaves as a stimulus signal rather than a property of one viewer's eyes, and it loaded below 0.15 on PC1 whether or not it was included. It is retained for later feature sets. The fits use the same 17, 14 and 18 recordings as the legacy pooled PCA.

Not yet applied: masking of windows where the tracker lost the eye. That flag comes from a rerun of the feature script and is absent from the current files.

2026-09-14

2. What PC1 reflects: correlation with ISC within each viewer

ISC was kept out of the PCA, which makes it an independent check on what the gaze axis captures. If high PC1 marks internally directed attention, windows high on PC1 should be windows in which the viewer's gaze has drifted from where the group is looking, so PC1 should correlate negatively with ISC. The correlation was computed at the level of the individual viewer's windows: for each recording, one Pearson r between its 236 PC1 scores and its 236 ISC values. Those per-recording correlations were then summarised across viewers, with a one-sample t-test on their Fisher-transformed values and a sign count. This was done for the PC1 of the pooled fit, evaluated within each video, and for each per-video fit's own PC1.

Raw ISC and ISC z-scored within the recording give exactly the same per-recording correlation, because a correlation is unchanged by shifting and scaling one variable within the same recording. One value per recording therefore covers both. The orientation step of the PCA fixes the overall sign to be negative, so the sign is not a finding; the size and consistency across viewers are.

Removing the part of ISC that all viewers share at the same moment of the film, by subtracting the group mean at each timepoint before correlating, changes the picture by video: in Hungarian the viewer-specific correlation is stronger than the raw one (-0.14, p 0.004), in English and Inscapes it is weaker (-0.04 to -0.07). So in Hungarian the axis tracks a viewer's own departures from the group's gaze, while in the other two films part of the link runs through scenes that everyone finds hard to follow. The table holds those values.

Reading: within a viewer, PC1 is weakly but consistently aligned with losing the group's gaze trajectory, sharing about 1% of its variance with ISC. It is not a synchrony measure in disguise. Whether the extreme windows on this axis are the ones where synchrony breaks down is a question for the label stage, not for a linear correlation.

2026-09-14

3. Mahalanobis deviation from the group

PC1 places each window on a within-viewer gaze axis. It says nothing about whether the viewer is behaving like everyone else at that moment of the film. The second ingredient is a group deviation: at each window, how far a viewer's eye behaviour sits from the other viewers watching the same scene. This is where ISC enters the feature set.

For each window, the viewer's nine features (the eight PCA features plus ISC) were compared with the mean of the other viewers of the same video at the same window. The difference vector was scaled by the inverse covariance of all such differences in that video, giving a Mahalanobis distance d. Distances were then z-scored within each recording, so that mahal_z means "unusual for this viewer", and separately within each timepoint, so that mahal_time_z means "unusual for this scene".

Two choices differ from the legacy computation. The group mean leaves the viewer out, so a person cannot be compared with a reference that contains themselves. With 14 to 18 viewers this changes almost nothing (r above 0.999 with the inclusive version), but it is the correct reference. Second, ISC is standardised across the video before the distance is computed. On its raw 0 to 1 scale its residual variance is about 0.015 against about 1 for the other features, and the covariance shrinkage used by the legacy code then reduces ISC's contribution to the squared distance from the nominal one ninth to about one thirtieth. With ISC on the same scale and an unshrunk covariance, which the sample size easily supports, every feature contributes exactly one ninth on average. The legacy deviation carries the same under-weighting of ISC.

What drives the extreme deviations

Averaged over all windows every feature contributes one ninth of the squared distance by construction, so only the extremes are informative. In each viewer's top 10% of windows by deviation, vergence variability carries 23% of the distance in the two narrative films, and vergence and its variability together carry a third in Inscapes, while saccade rate and pupil size contribute least. ISC contributes 6 to 9%. The large deviations remain mostly binocular events even with vergence taken from measured samples only, which means they are measured, not interpolated, and are left in place by design.

The stimulus accounts for 8 to 10% of the variance in deviation, less than for any single feature, which is expected since the group mean at each timepoint is removed. The distances are right-skewed, most strongly in English, so the within-viewer z of the deviation is dominated by a minority of large-deviation windows.

Reading: the deviation is a person-relative measure of departing from the group, concentrated at the internal pole of PC1 and carried mainly by vergence. The external pole sits at the group average. The seventh entry draws out what this means for the label rule.

2026-09-14

4. PC1 over time, by participant

Before building labels, a look at the raw material: each participant's PC1 score across the 236 windows of the film, for the pooled fit and for the per-video fit, with the group mean at each window drawn on top. The group mean is the stimulus-locked part of the axis, what the film does to everyone. The spread of the thin lines around it is the person-specific part, which is what a within-viewer label will be cut from.

2026-09-14

5. Recomputed features: vergence from measured samples, gaze-validity mask

The first pass of this track used the vergence series as stored in the vergence files, in which every sample where one or both eyes were lost is filled by linear interpolation. Those fills produce runs of outlying disparity up to three seconds long, and they were the main source of the extreme vergence windows. The features were recomputed with two changes, and every entry above now shows the recomputed results.

Vergence from measured samples only. Interpolated samples are excluded from the window mean and SD of vergence. A window with fewer than 30% measured samples gets no vergence value, and a recording whose median measured fraction is below one half contributes no vergence at all: NS194 and NS174_03 in English, NS174_03 in Hungarian, NS155 and NS210 in Inscapes. Measured samples are kept as they are, however extreme, so genuine or miscalibrated binocular events remain in the data by decision.

Gaze-validity mask. A window in which fewer than half the gaze samples were tracked has all eight gaze features set to missing, which places it at the recording median. Three Inscapes recordings, NS151, NS153 and NS155, have 92 to 106 such windows out of 236. In the first pass those windows carried features computed from whatever samples existed, and a window with little gaze has few detected saccades, which reads as low saccade rate, the internal pole of PC1.

The English fits use the 17 recordings of the legacy pooled PCA; the feature script's own list has four more, NS166, NS190 run 1 and 2, and NS193 run 1, which are excluded here for comparability.

What moved the Inscapes axis

To separate the two changes, the Inscapes per-video PCA was refit under each combination.

Both changes push in the same direction and they compound. Keeping the interpolated vergence but applying the mask lowers saccade rate from -0.39 to -0.11; keeping the mask off but using measured vergence lowers it to -0.27; dropping the masked windows from the fit instead of placing them at the median gives -0.37; and removing the three heavy-loss recordings altogether gives -0.27. No single choice restores the first-pass axis. The reading is that in Inscapes, once the vergence artefacts are gone and the no-gaze windows stop masquerading as low-saccade windows, the coherent within-viewer variation is binocular and pupillary rather than a saccade-and-blink trade-off. Whether that axis is the one to label states from in Inscapes is an open question, and it is now visible rather than hidden by the artefacts.

Downstream consequences

The PC1-to-ISC correlations weaken slightly, from means of -0.08 to -0.13 to -0.07 to -0.09, and the pooled fit evaluated in Hungarian is no longer significant on its own. The deviation-to-PC1 relation strengthens and becomes more uniform, from means of 0.17 to 0.37 to 0.26 to 0.30 with at most two negative recordings per video. Deviation extremes are still carried by vergence, now from measured samples. The monotone rise of deviation along PC1 is unchanged.

Not changed: the right-eye validity slip in the vergence routine, which affects the stored vergence files and needs those regenerated. The measured-sample rule is applied downstream of it. The loadings in the comparison table above are from the robust PCA at its default constant; the sixth and seventh entries explain why that constant was replaced.

2026-09-14

6. What the PCA is actually finding: two weak axes, not one

Two questions were put to the recomputed features: how stable the shared PC1 is, and whether each viewer's own PC1 would serve better. Answering them required checking the robust PCA itself, and that check changed the picture.

The robust PCA was shrinking the data away

The robust PCA used throughout, in the legacy chain and in this track, splits the feature matrix into a low-rank part and a sparse part and fits the PCA to the low-rank part. Its regularisation constant defaults to one over the square root of the number of rows, about 0.009 for 11,500 windows. At that value the sparse part is nearly free and absorbs 87% of the data's energy while being 91% nonzero; the low-rank part keeps 2 to 3.5% at rank about three. Every variance-explained figure reported for PC1 so far, 58 to 72%, was a share of that remnant. On the data itself PC1 explains about 20%. The direction survives roughly, with cosines of 0.86 to 0.95 against ordinary PCA, but the scores are projections of the shrunk part and correlate only 0.83 to 0.87 with the data projected on the same loadings. The legacy pooled fit has exactly this property; its stored loadings were reproduced to confirm it. A constant of 0.05 gives a genuinely sparse part, 0.3% of entries holding the spikes, and a PC1 within cosine 0.93 of ordinary PCA. Everything below uses ordinary PCA on the robust-standardised features.

Two nearly independent clusters

Within a viewer, the eight features form two groups that barely correlate with each other. Saccade rate and blink rate move against one another (r = -0.39). Vergence, its variability and pupil size move together (r = 0.30 to 0.38). Every other pair is below 0.2. Ordinary PCA returns these two groups as its first two components with almost equal variance, 20% and 17% against a uniform 12.5%, and which of them comes first depends on the sample: saccade-and-blink first in English, vergence-and-pupil first in Hungarian, Inscapes and the pooled fit. Because the two eigenvalues nearly tie, the per-video PC1 is unstable under resampling of recordings, with a bootstrap fifth-percentile cosine of 0.05 in English and 0.06 in Hungarian, meaning the two axes swap places. The pooled axis is steadier (fifth percentile 0.78) only because it has three times the recordings.

The legacy PC1, saccade rate -0.58 and blink rate +0.58 with vergence and pupil at 0.2 to 0.3, is a blend of the two clusters whose mix was set by the shrinkage rather than by the data. It is not the dominant direction of gaze behaviour; there is no dominant direction. There are two weak ones.

Subject-level PC1s

Each recording's own PC1 was fit on its 236 windows and compared with the shared axes. The own axis captures a median 33% of that recording's variance against 15 to 20% for the pooled axis, so it fits better by construction, but it is not a reliable object: the split-half cosine between an axis fit on the first half of a recording and one fit on the second half has a median of 0.29 to 0.47. Its cosine with the pooled axis has a median of 0.43 to 0.65 and is below 0.6 in 29 of 49 recordings. The feature that leads each viewer's axis is scattered across all eight, and in most cases it is simply whichever of the two clusters happened to be larger in that person's data. Subject-level axes would therefore assign different viewers to different constructs, and on 236 overlapping windows would not even reproduce within the same viewer.

Reading: the question is no longer pooled versus subject-level. It is whether an attention state should be defined by one axis at all. The data contain a saccade-blink axis and a vergence-pupil axis that are nearly independent within a viewer. A single PC1 will always be an arbitrary mix of them. The options are to treat the two as separate dimensions and define states in that plane, to pick one on theoretical grounds, or to reduce with a method that targets ISC or the neural data rather than variance. That decision is the next thing to settle.

2026-09-14

7. Robust PCA at lambda 0.05, and what it means for selecting states

The track now runs the robust PCA with its sparse-term weight set to 0.05 instead of the default 0.009. At this value the sparse part holds 0.25% of entries in the pooled fit and 1.4 to 2.0% per video, which is the spikes, and the low-rank part keeps 76 to 93% of the energy. PC1 is stated against the data: 20 to 23%, with PC2 at 18 to 20%. The axis is a near-even blend of the two clusters, and its cosine with the legacy PC1 on the same eight features is 0.955. So the legacy direction was a reasonable compromise arrived at by accident; this is the same compromise arrived at by a stated rule. All entries above were recomputed with it.

How PC1 combines the two clusters

Section 3 of the guide shows the eight features split into two groups that vary independently. A principal component is a single weighted sum, so it cannot represent two independent groups separately; it has to choose a mix. The mix it chooses is the one that maximises variance, and when the two groups have nearly equal variance the answer is to take both at once, because a sum of two independent signals has more variance than either alone. That is what the pooled PC1 does: it is 0.68 aligned with the saccade-blink axis and 0.66 with the vergence-pupil axis, an almost even split, and PC2 is the complementary combination, one cluster minus the other, at -0.67 and +0.62. Together the two components span the same plane as the two clusters; PCA has simply rotated the axes by about 45 degrees.

A window's PC1 score is therefore the sum of two things: how far its saccade-blink pattern has shifted toward fewer saccades and more blinks, and how far its vergence-pupil pattern has shifted toward higher vergence and a larger pupil, each relative to the person's usual level. A score of +1.5 can come from a large shift in one cluster with the other at normal, or a moderate shift in both. The score does not record which. In the pooled fit the two contribute about equally, 46 and 44 percent of the direction.

The per-video fits show that the even split is a property of the pooled sample, not of every film. English PC1 is 87 percent saccade-blink and only 5 percent vergence-pupil, so in English the "attention axis" is almost entirely saccades against blinks, and vergence-pupil moves to PC2. Hungarian is close to the pooled split. Inscapes leans the other way, 26 percent saccade-blink and 64 percent vergence-pupil. That ordering matches the sixth entry, where ordinary PCA put saccade-blink first in English and vergence-pupil first in Inscapes: the film changes which cluster carries more variance, and PC1 follows.

This is the practical reason the log keeps returning to the two-cluster option. The pooled PC1 gives every viewer the same axis, which is what a shared label needs, but the axis is an average of two things whose relative importance differs by film. Labelling on the two cluster scores directly would keep that information; labelling on PC1 averages it away.

Two things changed downstream, and both bear on how states should be identified.

The external pole is ordinary, the internal pole is unusual

With PC1 spanning both clusters, the group deviation is no longer monotone along it. It is lowest through the middle of the axis, about 0.3 SD below a viewer's average, returns to the viewer's average at the external extreme, and rises to about one SD above it at the internal extreme. Per viewer, the deviation correlates with PC1 at 0.36 to 0.44 and with its absolute value at 0.42 to 0.47. Windows at the external pole are not more like the group than average windows are; they are simply not far from it. Windows at the internal pole are far from it.

What the deviation gate does at each pole

For internal windows the deviation gate is informative: it keeps 41 to 46% of the PC1-extreme windows against a base rate of about 20%, so it is selecting a meaningfully different subset, and 12 to 15% of the windows it keeps owe their deviation to something PC1 does not measure, which in the third entry was mostly binocular events. For external windows the gate is close to uninformative: it keeps 31 to 35% against a base rate of 26 to 30%, so it is nearly a random subsample of the low-PC1 windows. The symmetric rule, high on both for internal and low on both for external, therefore does two different things at the two poles, and the external half of it mostly costs windows without changing what they are.

ISC

The per-viewer correlation of PC1 with ISC is -0.08 to -0.12, clearest in Inscapes and weakest in Hungarian, where it is not significant. Removing the stimulus-locked part of ISC strengthens the Hungarian relation to -0.14 and weakens the other two. The axis is aligned with losing the group's gaze, weakly, in all three films, but through different routes.

Reading, for the label rule. Three observations point the same way. Internal windows are the ones that are far along the axis and far from the group, and the deviation gate earns its place there. External windows are ordinary: at the group average, not below it, so a low-deviation requirement selects nothing in particular and a rule that treats the external pole as a mirror image of the internal one is describing a symmetry the data do not have. And the axis itself is a stated blend of two independent processes, saccade-blink and vergence-pupil, so a window's position on it can come from either. A rule that fits these facts would define internal by PC1 and deviation jointly, define external by PC1 alone or by a positive criterion such as high synchrony with the group, and either report which cluster carried each labelled window or label in the two-cluster plane directly. Any of these can be built from the files now on disk and tested against the neural contrasts.

2026-09-14

8. Deviation along PC1 at fine resolution, within viewer and within timepoint

The five-bin view in the third entry hides where the deviation starts to rise. Here PC1 is cut into bins of 0.1 between 0.4 and 1.0 and 0.2 elsewhere, and the mean deviation z per bin is averaged over viewers. The left panel uses the within-viewer scheme, PC1 and deviation each z-scored within a recording. The right panel uses the within-timepoint scheme, each z-scored across the viewers at the same window of the film, which asks whether a viewer is unusual for this scene rather than for themselves.

Gate behaviour by threshold

The same threshold applied to PC1 and to deviation, from 0.4 to 1.0. For internal windows the share passing the deviation gate is flat at 41 to 48% whatever the threshold, against a base rate that falls from 25 to 12%, so the gate is informative at every cut and increasingly so at higher ones. For external windows the share passing tracks the base rate down from 45% to 7%, and beyond 0.7 it is below the base rate: at that point requiring low deviation is worse than sampling low-PC1 windows at random. The mean deviation of windows above the threshold rises from about 0.5 at 0.4 to about 1.0 at 1.0, so a cut near 0.8 is where internal windows start to be clearly unusual.

Pass rates by threshold, both schemes

Reading: the deviation only begins to separate internal windows from ordinary ones above a PC1 z of about 0.8, and the label cut of 0.6 sits on the flat part of the curve. On the external side there is no threshold at which a low-deviation requirement selects anything the PC1 threshold has not already selected. Neither conclusion depends on whether the comparison is made within the viewer or within the timepoint.

2026-09-14

9. Which windows are likely internal, which are likely external

PC1 was cut into six regions chosen from the fine-bin curve of the previous entry: a far-external tail below -1.5, an external band from -1.5 to -0.4, the middle, an ambiguous band from 0.4 to 0.8 where the deviation has crossed the viewer's average but not risen, an internal band from 0.8 to 1.2, and a far-internal tail above 1.2. For each region and each viewer, the mean group deviation and the mean ISC were computed, then tested across viewers with one-sample t-tests against zero and paired t-tests between neighbouring regions. All measures are within-viewer z-scores unless marked.

What the regions look like in the features

The mean standardised value of each feature per region, averaged over viewers and then over the three videos, shows what a window in each region is made of. The internal bands are few saccades, many blinks, raised vergence and larger pupils, growing with distance along the axis. The external band is the same pattern reversed but at a fraction of the amplitude, which is why it is ordinary rather than extreme. The far-external tail is not simply more of the external band: its saccade rate is far above average while blink rate, vergence and pupil are barely below, so it is a burst of scanning with the other features near normal.

What each candidate rule selects

Six rules at the reported threshold, evaluated on what they select: the share of windows, the mean within-viewer ISC of the selected windows, and their mean within-timepoint deviation, that is how unusual they are for the scene. The ISC of the ISC-gated external rule is high by construction; its informative column is the deviation.

Reading. On the internal side, adding the deviation gate to a PC1 cut of 0.6 roughly doubles how unusual the selected windows are for the scene (within-timepoint deviation +0.6 to +1.5, p below 0.00001 in every video) and in English also lowers their ISC (-0.15 to -0.32, p 0.002). Raising the PC1 cut to 0.8 without a gate moves the deviation only modestly (+0.7 to +0.8) and leaves ISC unchanged, so the gate is doing more than a stricter cut would. On the external side, adding a low-deviation gate to a PC1 cut leaves ISC unchanged in every video (p 0.5 to 0.9): it makes the windows more scene-typical but no more synchronised, at the cost of two thirds of them. An ISC-based gate instead selects windows that are also somewhat more scene-typical (deviation -0.2 to -0.3, p 0.02 to 0.07). The evidence supports internal as a conjunction of PC1 and deviation, external as PC1 alone or PC1 with a synchrony criterion, and the far-external tail as a category to inspect rather than merge.

2026-09-14

10. The PC1 by deviation plane: where windows cluster and how the two measures combine

The previous entries treated PC1 as the primary axis and asked what the deviation adds along it. This entry looks at the two together as a plane. Each window is a point with PC1 z on one axis and deviation z on the other, both within viewer. Three questions: where do the windows sit, are there discrete groups in the plane or one continuous cloud, and how much does each measure tell you about the other in each direction.

Are there discrete groups?

Gaussian mixtures with one to four components were fit to the plane. Moving from one component to two lowers the Bayesian information criterion by 4 to 7%, and further components add well under 1%. The two-component solution is the same in every film: a large component holding 61 to 75% of windows centred near PC1 -0.2 to -0.3 and deviation -0.3 to -0.5, and a smaller component holding 25 to 39% centred near PC1 +0.5 to +0.7 and deviation +0.8 to +1.0. When a third component is allowed it splits the large one along PC1 into an external band and a middle band at the same low deviation; it never produces a low-PC1, low-deviation lobe distinct from the ordinary mass. The plane therefore contains one candidate state, the internal lobe, and a continuum for everything else. Since the two lobes overlap heavily, the mixture is a description of shape, not a classifier.

Each measure conditioned on the other

Within a viewer, the correlation between deviation and PC1 is 0.34 to 0.41 overall, but it is not uniform. Restricted to windows with PC1 above the viewer's median it is 0.51 to 0.60, positive in every recording; restricted to windows below the median it is -0.14 to -0.19, weakly negative because the deviation turns back up in the far-external tail. On the internal side the two measures are close to one dimension; on the external side they are nearly independent.

The reverse conditional makes the same point from the deviation's side. Among windows with deviation z above 2, 65 to 71% have PC1 above 0.6; among windows with deviation below -1, only 5 to 10% do. So a large deviation on its own is a strong indication of an internal window. The probability of PC1 below -0.6 barely moves across deviation bins, from about 30 to 38% at low deviation to 13 to 17% at high, so the deviation says little about whether a window is external.

Per-viewer rates under candidate rules

Windows per viewer, out of 236, selected by each rule; mean, SD and range across viewers. A usable rule should give every viewer a workable number of windows and should not let the count swing from zero to fifty between people for reasons unrelated to attention.

Reading. PC1 and deviation cluster together on the internal side and only there: above the viewer's median PC1 they rise together at r 0.5 to 0.6, the mixture finds a lobe centred at high values of both, and a large deviation alone points to a high-PC1 window two times out of three. An internal state defined by both is therefore a single coherent region of the plane, and either measure could stand in for the other there, with the conjunction selecting its core. On the external side there is no second lobe, the correlation is near zero, and deviation carries no information about PC1. The conjunction rule for external gives 20 to 24 windows per viewer with a range of 0 to 53, against 65 to 70 with a range of 49 to 82 for PC1 alone; the low-deviation gate is what makes the count erratic. The external state is best defined as the low side of the ordinary mass, by PC1 alone, and any refinement of it should come from a measure that does vary across that side, such as synchrony, rather than from the deviation.

2026-09-14

11. ISC as a third criterion: does it structure the external side?

The previous entry found that the deviation carries no information about which low-PC1 windows are external. The natural alternative is ISC, since an externally attentive viewer should be tracking the group. The question is whether ISC does on the external side what the deviation does on the internal side: rise systematically as PC1 moves toward the pole, and form a lobe with it. Tested with within-viewer ISC and with within-timepoint ISC, the latter asking whether the viewer is more synchronised than the others at that scene.

Does ISC form a lobe with low PC1?

Gaussian mixtures on the PC1 by ISC plane improve on a single component by only 0.4 to 2.9% of BIC (against 4 to 7% for PC1 by deviation), and in three dimensions, PC1, deviation and ISC together, the second component is the same internal lobe as before with ISC contributing nothing to its separation. No low-PC1, high-ISC group exists in any film.

ISC as a gate on external candidates

Among windows with PC1 below -0.6, the share with within-viewer ISC above 0.6 is 3 to 6 points above the base rate, and with within-timepoint ISC above 0.6 it equals the base rate. Both gates are as uninformative as the deviation gate was. What they do change is which windows are kept: ISC-gated external windows are somewhat more scene-typical, with within-timepoint deviation of -0.2 to -0.3 against -0.1 to -0.16 for PC1 alone. That was already visible in the ninth entry. The within-timepoint ISC gate also makes the per-viewer count erratic, 0 to 61 windows, because some viewers are below the group's synchrony at nearly every scene.

Reading: ISC does not cluster with PC1 on the external side any more than the deviation does. The external side is homogeneous on all three measures: a viewer at PC1 -1.2 is not more synchronised, nor closer to the group, than one at -0.5. ISC belongs in the pipeline as an independent check on what a label selects, and as a positive criterion if an external state is meant to be "synchronised with the group" by definition, but it is not a second dimension that sharpens the external pole the way deviation sharpens the internal one. The asymmetry stands: internal is a conjunction, external is a threshold on the axis.

12. First neural contrast under the track's labels

The most direct test: the same two-stage mixed-model contrast the legacy pipeline reports (per-contact Internal minus External amplitude, then a mixed model with person as a random effect, FDR within video across the region by band matrix), run with the track's conj labels at threshold 0.6. Internal is a high axis score and a high group deviation; External is a low axis score between -1.5 and -0.6. Windows below -1.5, the far-external tail, carry a separate label that the contrast script does not read, so they are excluded from both state means in the same way neutral windows are; they are neither Internal nor External. Everything upstream differs from legacy as documented above: measured-only vergence, gaze-validity mask, robust PCA at lambda 0.05, ISC out of the PCA. The comparison run is the legacy primary, symmetric rule at 0.6 on the legacy features. Both use the mean window statistic, stride 1, and the pipeline's neural inclusion list of 42 recordings (16 English, 13 Hungarian, 13 Inscapes), which is smaller than the 49 used on the eye side: seven eye-included recordings are not in the neural list.

Each heatmap is one film: rows are networks, columns are frequency bands from delta to HFA, colour is the mixed-model z for Internal minus External, blue positive, red negative. A dot marks cells significant at FDR 0.05. A black outline marks the hypothesis cells: alpha up in dorsal attention, visual and default networks; gamma and HFA down in dorsal attention and visual; theta up in default. Reading. The track's labels reproduce the legacy pattern where it was strongest and change it where the eye data said the legacy rule was weakest. On Y17 raw, Inscapes improves from 5 hits and 3 contradictions to 8 hits and none; Hungarian goes from 5 hits and 3 contradictions to 6 and 3 with more significant cells overall; English keeps its clean direction, 4 hits and no contradictions, with fewer significant cells, 17 against 29. 13. Neural amplitude across the six states, far external to far internal

The contrast in the previous entry compares two labelled states. This entry shows the whole axis. Every window was assigned to one of six PC1 regions, using PC1 alone so that the profile shows the axis itself rather than the deviation gate. The regions are those of the ninth entry with one change made on 2026-09-15: the internal region starts at PC1 z 0.6 rather than 0.8, because under the by-timepoint deviation the rise begins near 0.5 (entry 8), so the bands are far external below -1.5, external -1.5 to -0.4, middle -0.4 to 0.4, ambiguous 0.4 to 0.6, internal 0.6 to 1.2 and far internal above 1.2. For each contact, the mean robust-z amplitude in each region was taken and the contact's mean over all its kept windows subtracted, so that a value of +0.05 means "this contact runs 0.05 SD above its own average when the viewer is in this region". Bad windows are excluded as in the contrast. Bars are the mean across contacts with the standard error; the first figure averages across networks with equal weight, and the folded figures give every network.

Planned contrasts over the six regions

Rather than testing the fifteen pairs among six categories, two planned contrasts per network and band. The trend is each contact's weighted least-squares slope of its six region means on region rank 1 to 6, tested across contacts with a mixed model and a person random intercept; a positive slope means amplitude rises from external to internal along the whole axis. The endpoint contrast is far internal minus far external per contact, same second stage. In the seven hypothesis networks the trend is reported uncorrected; every other test is FDR-corrected within its network-and-film cell over the twelve tests run there. On the panels above, a significant trend is drawn as the fitted slope line across the six bars, black rising and red falling, with stars at its right end; a significant endpoint contrast is drawn as a comparison bracket from the far-external bar to the far-internal bar with stars. Both carry z and p on hover. Results are saved as state_profile/trend6[_gated|_gated_tp].csv.

14. Three collapsed states and pairwise contrasts

The six regions collapse to three: External (PC1 z below -0.4, the far-external tail included), Middle (-0.4 to 0.6, the ambiguous band included) and Internal (0.6 and above, the far-internal tail included; the edge was 0.8 before 2026-09-15, see entry 13). Per contact the collapsed means are window-count weighted. For every network and band the three pairwise differences, Internal minus External, Internal minus Middle, Middle minus External, are tested with the pipeline's two-stage model: a per-contact difference, then a mixed model with a person random intercept.

Correction scheme. Seven hypothesis networks were fixed in advance: Y7 dorsal attention, default mode and visual; Y17 Dorsal Attention A, Default A, Visual Central and Visual Peripheral. In those, the Internal minus External contrast is reported uncorrected across the six bands. Every other test, meaning all contrasts in the remaining networks and the Internal minus Middle and Middle minus External contrasts in the hypothesis networks, is FDR-corrected within its network-and-film cell, so the correction count is the number of tests run in that network for that film. A filled marker over a bar pair means significant under whichever rule applies to it.

Internal versus External in the hypothesis networks

PC1-only states first, then gated on within-subject deviation, then with a timepoint-relative internal gate and the same within-subject external gate.

On the third row. At 0.6 the timepoint-relative internal gate is as strict as the within-subject one: 21 to 22% of all windows pass it against 20 to 23%, and 47 to 49% of internal candidates against 48 to 52%, so the two rows are matched in strictness and the threshold is not the issue. The two gates agree on about 40% of candidates and each keeps a further 10% the other rejects. What differs is the distribution across people: a viewer who sits further from the group than the others at most scenes passes the timepoint gate almost always, and one who tracks the group closely almost never, so per-viewer pass rates range from 0.05 to 0.93 against 0.19 to 0.72 for the within-subject gate, and internal windows per viewer in Inscapes range from 2 to 41 against 12 to 33. The within-subject z removes that between-person trait by construction. The third row is therefore a sensitivity, not a candidate primary; a person-balanced timepoint-relative definition would gate on both deviations at once.

Reading. The direction is uniform: positive. The hypothesised negative gamma and HFA in dorsal attention appears only as one uncorrected gamma cell in English Dorsal Attention A; elsewhere gamma and HFA are positive where significant, in Default A and Visual Peripheral in Hungarian. 16. Methodological justification: a single gaze axis, with its components reported

Draft text for the methods, written from the analyses in this log. Numbers refer to the recomputed features (entry 5) and the robust PCA at lambda 0.05 (entry 7).

Structure of the eye-movement features

Eight window-level eye-movement features (saccade rate, saccade dispersion, vergence, vergence variability, blink rate, blink duration, pupil size and pupil variability) were standardised within each recording before any dimension reduction, so that all subsequent quantities describe deviations from a viewer's own typical behaviour. Across the 11,564 windows of the 49 recordings, the within-viewer correlation structure of these features was sparse. Three pairs exceeded |r| = 0.2: saccade rate with blink rate (r = -0.39), vergence with vergence variability (r = 0.38) and vergence with pupil size (r = 0.30). All remaining pairs, including every pair crossing between these groups, lay between -0.10 and 0.17. The features therefore formed two groups, a saccade-blink group and a vergence-pupil group, that co-varied within themselves but not with each other. Composite scores for the two groups (blink rate minus saccade rate; vergence plus vergence variability plus pupil size) correlated at a mean of r = 0.08 within viewers. Ordinary principal component analysis recovered the two groups as its first two components with 20.3% and 17.1% of the variance, and the order of the two reversed between films (saccade-blink first in the English condition; vergence-pupil first in the Hungarian and Inscapes conditions), as expected when two independent sources of comparable variance are present.

Why a single axis is used

A state label requires a quantity that is defined identically for every viewer and every film. Principal components do not satisfy this requirement here: because the two feature groups carry nearly equal variance, the first component of any given fit is whichever mixture of them happened to be largest in that sample, and the per-film first components decomposed differently onto the two groups (English: 87% saccade-blink, 5% vergence-pupil; Hungarian: 44% and 39%; Inscapes: 26% and 64%). The second component is correspondingly a different quantity in each film. Using the first two components as two attention dimensions would therefore assign different constructs to different films, and there is no empirical basis for treating the second component as an attention axis: the evidence relating gaze to attention (below) concerns the direction in which both groups shift together, not the direction in which one shifts relative to the other.

The pooled first component, fit across all recordings, is an approximately even combination of the two groups (cosine 0.68 with the saccade-blink axis and 0.66 with the vergence-pupil axis). We retain this pooled axis as the single gaze dimension on which states are defined, for three reasons. First, it is fixed: the same weights apply to every window of every viewer in every film, so a score has one meaning throughout. Second, it is stable under resampling of recordings (leave-one-recording-out cosine with the full axis at least 0.97), whereas per-film and per-viewer axes are not (bootstrap fifth-percentile cosine 0.05 to 0.06 in the narrative films; split-half cosine of within-viewer axes 0.29 to 0.47). Third, and decisively, the two feature groups relate to independent markers of attentional state in the same direction, so their sum is a legitimate composite rather than an arbitrary mixture. Within viewers, the saccade-blink score correlated with gaze inter-subject correlation at a mean of r = -0.09 and the vergence-pupil score at r = -0.05, both negative in the majority of recordings; their combination correlated at r = -0.11, and with the Mahalanobis distance from the group at r = 0.42, exceeding either group alone (0.23 and 0.36). A shift toward fewer saccades, more blinks, higher vergence and a larger pupil is thus associated, through either route, with reduced tracking of the group's gaze and increased departure from the group's behaviour, which is the operational signature of internally directed attention adopted here.

Why the components are nonetheless reported

Because the axis is a sum of two independent processes, a given score does not record which process produced it, and the relative contribution of the two differs by film. To keep this visible, each labelled window additionally carries the two group scores, and state contrasts are reported for the composite axis and, as a sensitivity analysis, for labels derived from each group score alone. Agreement between the three establishes that the composite is not driven by one group in one film; disagreement identifies the group responsible. This preserves the single shared axis that a cross-film comparison requires while making its composition auditable.

Consequences for the labelling rule

The relation between the gaze axis and the group deviation is asymmetric. Binning the within-viewer axis score showed that windows through the middle and external range of the axis lie about 0.3 SD closer to the group than the viewer's average, that the deviation reaches the viewer's average near a score of 0.4 to 0.5, and that it rises only above about 0.8, reaching one SD beyond average above 1.2. Within viewers, the correlation between deviation and axis score was 0.51 to 0.60 on the internal half of the axis and -0.14 to -0.19 on the external half, and a two-component Gaussian mixture on the axis-by-deviation plane isolated a single lobe centred at high values of both (25 to 39% of windows) against an ordinary mass, with no low-axis, low-deviation group in any film. Where a label rule combines two conditions, the second condition acts as a filter on the windows the first selects; its informativeness was quantified as the difference, computed within each viewer and tested across viewers, between the fraction of axis-selected windows that satisfy it and the fraction of all that viewer's windows that satisfy it (the base rate, which is what an unrelated criterion of the same strictness would pass). A deviation criterion adds information for internal labels: 42 to 47% of axis-selected windows satisfied it against a base rate of 20 to 23%, a difference of 22 to 26 points that was positive in 48 of 49 viewers (paired p below 0.0001 in each film). It adds little for external labels: 30 to 34% satisfied it against a base rate of 26 to 30%, a difference of 2 to 4 points (paired p = 0.05, 0.41 and 0.24), where it also left the ISC of the selected windows unchanged (paired p = 0.5 to 0.9 across viewers), and where it made the per-viewer count of external windows erratic (0 to 53 against 49 to 82 for the axis alone). Gaze synchrony was tested as a substitute criterion and behaved the same way: within viewers, ISC was uncorrelated with the axis score on its external half (r = -0.04 to +0.04, all p greater than 0.1), showed no gradient across external bins, formed no low-axis, high-ISC group in mixture fits (BIC improvement 0.4 to 2.9% against 4 to 7% for the deviation plane), and passed external candidates at or near the base rate (within-viewer ISC 0 to 6 points above base, paired p = 0.12, 0.94 and 0.007, the last in Inscapes; within-timepoint ISC at base). The external side of the axis is therefore homogeneous on deviation, on ISC and on scene-relative ISC. Internal states are defined by the conjunction of a high axis score and a high group deviation; external states by a low axis score alone. Where an external state is intended to mean synchrony with the group by definition, an ISC criterion may be added as a positive definition, with the understanding that it selects windows that are more scene-typical (within-timepoint deviation -0.2 to -0.3 against -0.1 to -0.16, p = 0.02 to 0.07) at the cost of roughly half the windows, and that its within-timepoint form is unstable across viewers. Windows in the extreme external tail (axis score below -1.5, about 4% of windows) were more distant from the group than the adjacent external band in all three films (paired p = 0.04 to 0.0001) and consisted of elevated saccade rate with the remaining features near normal; they are treated as a separate category pending inspection rather than merged into the external state.

2026-09-14

17. The chain of inference: what the analyses establish and what they assume

The mixture model, the base-rate comparisons and the binned curves are three descriptions of the same cloud of windows. None of them knows what "internal" or "external" means. The meaning is attached by a chain of three links, of which only the second and third can be checked against data.

Link 1. The direction of the axis is an assumption

PC1 was oriented so that high scores correspond to fewer saccades, more blinks, higher vergence and a larger pupil. That end was declared the internal end because those signatures are the ones the literature associates with disengagement from a visual stimulus, and the orientation step used ISC to fix the sign. Nothing in this log tests the assumption. If it were wrong, every statement below would remain true as a description of the plane, and the words internal and external would simply be attached to the wrong ends.

Link 2. The plane is structured, and the structure is at one end

This is what the analyses establish, from three angles that agree. The mixture model finds one ordinary mass and one lobe, and the lobe sits at high PC1 and high deviation, in every film (entry 10). The base-rate comparison finds that among high-PC1 windows a high deviation is twice as common as it is overall, while among low-PC1 windows a low deviation is no more common than overall (entry 8, tested per viewer in the justification). The binned curve finds that deviation rises with PC1 only above about 0.8 (entry 8). All three say that there is a region where windows are jointly extreme on both measures, and that it lies at the high end only. This is a fact about the data, tested across viewers, and it does not depend on what the ends are called.

Link 3. The lobe behaves the way an internal state should

This connects the structure to the label. Windows in the lobe have lower ISC than the viewer's average, -0.20 to -0.25 in the far-internal band (entry 9), and they are further from the other viewers' behaviour at the same scene. Both are what disengagement from a shared stimulus should produce, and neither was built into the axis: ISC was excluded from the PCA, and the deviation is a separate calculation over nine features. So the lobe is not merely a dense region; it is a dense region whose members track the group less. That is evidence, though modest, that the label at that end means what it is meant to mean.

What the external side lacks

No lobe (entry 10), conditional rates at base for deviation and for ISC (entries 8 and 11), and no variation of ISC along that side (entry 11). The external label therefore rests on link 1 alone: these windows are at the opposite end of an axis whose high end has been checked. They are ordinary windows, and external is the name for being ordinary on this axis. That is a defensible definition, but it is a definition rather than a finding, and it is weaker than the internal one. This is why the justification defines internal by a conjunction and external by the axis alone: the conjunction is where the evidence is.

What would close the chain

The neural data. If windows in the lobe show a cortical signature that differs from ordinary windows in the direction predicted for internally directed attention, link 1 gains support from outside the eye data. The analyses in this log tell you which rule yields the cleanest set of lobe windows to run that test on. They cannot tell you what the lobe is.

Summary of the standing of each claim. "PC1 and deviation are jointly extreme only at the high end": established, tested across viewers. "The high end has lower ISC and greater group departure": established, modest effect sizes. "The high end is internally directed attention": assumed from the eye-movement literature and the ISC orientation, awaiting neural confirmation. "The low end is externally directed attention": defined as the complement, not independently supported.
